name: Maryland bridge

image.caption: Bridge (dentistry)
image.creator: The original uploader was Wagonerj at English Wikipedia.

lead: A Maryland bridge replaces a missing tooth, often a front tooth, with a false tooth carrying metal or ceramic wings that are glued behind the adjacent teeth. The gap is visibly closed once it is placed.

The wings are bonded to acid-etched enamel on the back surface of neighbouring teeth, holding the replacement tooth in the gap. It needs little or no preparation, so it preserves more natural tooth than a conventional bridge.

paras: It is used as a conservative way to fill a gap, especially at the front. Designs with a single wing on one side (cantilever) are reported to have fewer complications than designs bonded on both sides.
Debonding is the main concern and can let decay start under a loose wing. It is not suited to people who grind their teeth, have mobile teeth or have a nickel allergy.

angle.text: People missing a tooth use a Maryland bridge to fill the gap with little drilling of neighbouring teeth. The bonded wings hold a replacement tooth in place and the gap is closed once placed; debonding is the usual failure noted.

lead: A Maryland bridge, also called a resin-bonded, adhesive or etched-cast bridge, replaces a missing tooth with a false tooth (pontic) held in place by thin metal or ceramic 'wings' bonded to the backs of the neighbouring teeth, so little or no drilling of those teeth is needed.[1][2] For appearance, it closes a visible gap in the smile, most often a single front tooth, with a fixed, tooth-coloured replacement that can be shaped and shaded to match the teeth beside it.[1][3]

The route to a better-looking smile runs through conservation. Because the abutment teeth keep their natural enamel and outline, the neighbours stay unaltered while the gap is closed, and a pontic of the right length, width and shade restores the line of the smile.[1][3] Dental reviews describe the resin-bonded bridge as a tooth-saving option when adjacent teeth are relatively sound, and list it beside the conventional bridge and the implant as one of three standard choices for single-tooth replacement.[4][5]

The design grew out of the acid-etch bonding revolution of the 1970s and 1980s. An early perforated-wing version was described by Alain Rochette in 1973, and the etched cast-metal bridge that carries the 'Maryland' name was the subject of clinical reviews by 1988.[2][6] Reviews of the published literature report five-year success rates of roughly 84 to 88 percent for resin-bonded bridges overall, and randomized trials and registered studies continue to compare designs and materials.[7][8] Debonding of a wing is the usual failure mode and the main practical topic in the literature.[1][4]

The name sometimes causes confusion online: 'Maryland bridge' refers only to this dental prosthesis, and in everyday dental language it is used loosely for resin-bonded bridges of several metal and ceramic designs.[2][3]

paras: A resin-bonded bridge is an artificial tooth bonded to one or two abutment teeth. If it is built directly in the mouth from composite resin, the connector between pontic and abutment is the weakest part; the alternative is an indirect bridge in which a metal, fibre-reinforced composite or ceramic framework spans the space, is made in a dental laboratory and is bonded with composite cement.[3][9] The name 'Maryland bridge' is commonly used for the etched cast-metal version, and a 1988 clinical review described it under that name.[2]

Reviewers describe the guiding principle as minimal invasiveness: unlike a conventional bridge, which needs the neighbouring teeth to be cut down for crowns, the resin-bonded bridge relies on adhesion to etched enamel.[1][9] A Dutch review nevertheless notes that some preparation is usually made, because a restoration on an abutment tooth needs a certain amount of occlusal space, and that resistance features such as grooves and rests can improve the longevity of the bridge.[3][9]

Wikipedia's bridge article notes that retainer wings bond to etched enamel, that abutments need little or no preparation and are best when intact, and that connectors should be at least 0.7 mm wide and 2 mm high, with the pontic lightly touching the opposing tooth in the bite but not in side-to-side movement.[1]

Designs include fixed-fixed (a wing on each side of the gap), fixed-movable and cantilever (a single wing).[1] The cantilever is the most tooth-conserving, is the design of choice for single front teeth and is easy to clean, but its small bonding area limits retention and exposes it to torquing forces.[1] Fixed-fixed designs offer large bonding surfaces and simple laboratory work, but equal retention on both abutments is hard to achieve, particularly at the back of the mouth; fixed-movable designs let the abutments move independently but are not advised for front teeth or long spans.[1]

Materials include cast base-metal alloys (the classic Maryland bridge), zirconia, lithium disilicate, In-Ceram alumina and fibre-reinforced composite.[7] Ceramic frameworks are an alternative to metal ones, and zirconia and lithium-disilicate versions are the subject of registered trials.[10][11][12] Direct composite bridges, sometimes reinforced with fibre, are made chairside and are described as suited to the immediate replacement of a lost front tooth.[9][13]

Resin-retained bridgework followed the introduction of enamel etching and composite cements. Alain Rochette described a resin-retained splint in 1973 in which the metal retainer was perforated with countersunk holes that locked into the composite cement; the Rochette bridge was popular in the 1970s and later declined as improved cements and treatment of the metal's inner surface gave better retention without perforating the wing.[6]

The etched cast-metal bridge, in which the inner surface of the metal casting is roughened electrolytically before cementing, came to be known as the Maryland bridge. By 1988 a clinical review in the Journal of Dentistry described its use, and papers in 1989 tested retainer designs and published clinical guidelines.[2][14][15] A 1993 paper reported clinical techniques and long-term results for the etched cast restoration, and another that year described immediate replacement of incisors with cantilevered adhesive bridgework.[16][13] Later work turned to ceramic frameworks and single-retainer cantilevers.[17][12]

Indications described in the literature include replacing a single tooth where the neighbours are sound and unrestored, where gum health is stable, and where a patient is unsuited to or not ready for an implant; a registered trial has examined anterior resin-bonded restorations in adolescents.[1][18] Wikipedia also lists splinting periodontally compromised teeth and fixed retention after orthodontic treatment among the uses.[1]

Ridge-lap pontics, which sit against the gum and mimic a tooth emerging from it, are described as offering the most natural look among pontic styles, while hygienic and bullet pontics are easier to clean but look less natural.[1] A resin-bonded bridge can also serve as a temporary: a randomized trial in China compared a fibre-reinforced resin-bonded bridge placed a week after implant surgery with later restoration in 23 patients missing a front tooth, and a 2020 randomized trial examined placing a Maryland bridge on non-submerged implants to preserve marginal bone.[19][20]
Case reports describe the same approach after trauma, for example using glass-fibre-reinforced composite to manage an avulsed central incisor.[21]

Wikipedia contrasts resin-bonded bridges with conventional bridges: a conventional bridge needs crowns on the abutment teeth, which means more tooth preparation and a higher risk of pulp damage, while conventional fixed-fixed bridges offer maximum strength and are the most accepted design for longer spans.[1] Advantages given for resin-bonded designs include conservation of tooth structure (especially with single-retainer cantilevers), simple laboratory construction for fixed-fixed versions and easy cleaning for cantilevers.[1]

A Dutch review of single-tooth replacement states that the choice among conventional bridge, resin-bonded bridge and single implant depends on the patient's dentition and preferences, that the resin-bonded bridge is the cheapest of the three, that the bridge can loosen at an inconvenient moment and need recementing or replacing, and that an implant has several advantages but requires an experienced clinician; orthodontic closure of the space is another option for young patients.[4] A 2013 Dutch review calls the resin-bonded bridge cost-effective both financially and biologically, noting that longevity is limited but that when it fails the consequences for the abutment teeth are generally limited and other treatments remain available.[9]

Dental sources advise good oral hygiene around any bridge because plaque can cause gum inflammation, cleaning under the pontic with interdental aids, regular review appointments, and treating decay or gum disease before and after placement.[1] Because a debonded wing may go unnoticed, regular checks are part of follow-up.[1]

Debonding is the main failure mode, and a wing that has come loose without being noticed can allow decay to develop beneath it.[1] Contraindications listed include bruxism or other parafunction, mobile teeth, malaligned teeth, abutments with little enamel or heavy restorations, nickel allergy, and active caries or periodontal disease.[1]

A literature review of single-retainer anterior bridges examined whether material choice changes survival, and a Dutch review notes there is disagreement over whether two-unit versions outperform three-unit ones.[17][3] Reviewers also say that the moderate results of some resin-bonded bridges have been associated with insufficient preparation of the abutment teeth.[3]

A systematic review of human trials and cohort studies searched three databases from 1965 to March 2017 and reported an estimated five-year success rate of 88.18 percent for metal-framework resin-bonded bridges and 84.41 percent for non-metal frameworks (zirconia 92.07 percent, In-Ceram alumina 94.26 percent, fibre-reinforced composite 84.83 percent). Success was defined as the bridge remaining in place without debonding, biological failure or mechanical failure. Failure rates did not differ significantly between single, double and multiple retainers, and technical complications were the leading cause of failure.[7]

A 2018 review of single-retainer (cantilever) anterior bridges searched the English-language literature to May 2016 and examined whether the framework material affected survival.[17] A long-term randomized trial compared cantilevered with fixed-fixed bridges for missing upper incisors, and a 2020 randomized trial of molar replacement compared two-unit cantilevers with three-unit fixed-movable designs.[8][22] A randomized trial of five-year survival of posterior adhesive bridges examined the influence of bonding systems and tooth preparation.[23]

Registered trials include a 78-participant study of two-unit cantilever bridges for missing molars started in 2014, a 40-participant proof-of-concept study of all-ceramic zirconia bridges started in 2016, a 90-participant trial of no-preparation bridges, a 44-participant comparison of lithium-disilicate and zirconia single-retainer bridges started in 2023, and a study of anterior resin-bonded restorations in adolescents.[24][10][25][11][18] Earlier randomized work compared patients receiving bilateral resin-bonded bridges for a shortened dental arch with those receiving conventional partial dentures, looking at nutrient intake.[26]

lore.intro: Maryland bridges are discussed mainly in dental practice and patient-information settings; in looksmaxxing and smile-improvement circles they come up as a lower-cost, lower-preparation alternative to implants or crowned bridges for a missing front tooth.

claims.claim: A Maryland bridge saves the neighbouring teeth because they are barely cut
It is a cheaper route to a replacement front tooth than an implant
A single-wing cantilever is the best design for a front tooth
Ceramic frameworks look more natural and last as long as metal
A Maryland bridge can hold the space temporarily while an implant heals
People who grind their teeth should avoid them

timeline.event: Alain Rochette describes a resin-retained splint with perforated metal wings, the forerunner of the Rochette bridge.[6]
Clinical review of the etched cast metal resin-bonded (Maryland) bridge appears in the Journal of Dentistry.[2]
Studies of retainer design for etched resin-bonded bridges and Australian clinical guidelines for resin-bonded prostheses are published.[14][15]
Papers report long-term results of etched cast restorations and cantilevered adhesive bridgework for incisors.[16][13]
Dutch reviews and a randomized study compare single-tooth replacement options and posterior adhesive bridges.[4][23]
A randomized trial of two-unit cantilever resin-bonded bridges for missing molars begins (NCT02239718).[24]
Long-term randomized trial of cantilevered versus fixed-fixed bridges for upper incisors is published; zirconia bridge proof-of-concept trial begins.[8][11]
Systematic review reports five-year success rates of about 88% (metal) and 84% (non-metal).[7]
Trial comparing lithium disilicate with zirconia single-retainer bridges for a missing front tooth begins.[10]
Dutch review of resin-bonded bridges in the anterior area is published.[3]
